title: The Emperor's New Clothes
text:
An emperor cared about nothing so much as fine clothes. Two swindlers came to his city, claiming to be weavers of a marvelous cloth. Not only was it beautiful, they said, but it had a special property: it was invisible to anyone who was unfit for his position or hopelessly stupid.

The emperor paid them handsomely, and they set up empty looms and pretended to work. He sent his honest old minister to inspect. The minister saw nothing, but he did not dare say so, in case it meant he was unfit for office, and he praised the colors and pattern. A second official did the same. Finally the emperor went himself. He saw nothing either, but since everyone around him admired the cloth, he admired it too.

On the day of the great procession, the swindlers pretended to dress him, and he walked through the streets under a canopy while the chamberlains held up a train that did not exist. The crowds cheered the beautiful clothes, because no one wanted to be thought a fool.

Then a small child said, "But he hasn't got anything on!" The words passed from person to person until the whole crowd was saying it. The emperor felt they were right, but he decided the procession must go on, and he walked even more proudly, with his chamberlains carrying the invisible train.
lesson: Groups can agree to a falsehood because each person fears looking foolish alone. Make it safe for someone to say the obvious, and say it yourself when you see it.
people: The emperor, two swindlers, ministers, a child
source: Hans Christian Andersen, The Emperor's New Clothes (Keiserens nye Klaeder), 1837
